gluttony

/GLUHT-uh-nee/ - the stress falls on GLUHT · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Gluttony means overindulgence in food or drink.

After a week of holiday gluttony, even the dog turned down table scraps.

Worked Example

Thanksgiving at Uncle Ray's follows a script: a third plate after the second, a fourth wedge of pie 'to even out the pan,' the belt loosened one hole at a time, and then the long groan from the couch. Nobody at that table is hungry past two o'clock. What happens after two is gluttony.

Gluttony is the right word because appetite has an end and this eating doesn't respect it. Appetite is the body's honest wanting; gluttony begins where want ends and the indulging keeps going — plates after fullness, driven by the pleasure of excess itself.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

overindulgence: Overindulgence is too much of any pleasure — screens, spending, sleep, sweets. Gluttony is overindulgence kept to the table: eating and drinking carried on past fullness. Every bout of gluttony is overindulgence, but only the food-and-drink kind earns the older, harsher word.

greediness: Greediness is grasping for more of anything — money, food, praise — and hoarding it whether or not it can ever be used. Gluttony is narrower and bodily: the excess is eaten and drunk on the spot. The greedy keep what they gain; the glutton swallows it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

moderation: keeping appetites inside sensible limits

abstinence: going without entirely — the far shore from gluttony

Where it sits · how far past need the eating goes — appetite → indulgence → gluttony

appetite vs. gluttony: Appetite is the body's honest wanting, and it switches off when fed; gluttony is what keeps eating after the switch.

indulgence vs. gluttony: An indulgence is one knowing step past need — dessert on a Tuesday; gluttony makes excess the whole meal, and the meal after that.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — glutton-

Root — glutton-: one who gulps (Latin glutto)

Suffix — -y

Suffix — -y: state or habit of

Put it together

Put it together: Glutton- (a gulper — Latin glutto, from gluttire, 'to swallow') + -y (the state of being one) = the gulper's habit. The Latin verb is very nearly onomatopoeia: you can hear the swallow in glut-. Gluttony is swallowing raised from reflex to lifestyle.

Use the root in a new word: glut

Word Choice

formal / moralizing

Gluttony carries the weight of the old list of deadly sins — it judges, and it stays at the table: food and drink. Insatiable, its unit-mate, names a different condition: hunger (for anything — praise, facts, profit) that no amount ever satisfies. The glutton overshoots fullness; the insatiable never reach it.
